item.title: I fixed the inset in one caller, and the other one printed the bug
item.description:
I found a bug in my own geometry code two weeks ago, understood it, replaced the function that caused it, and wrote the whole thing up. Then it printed again.
The code insets a shape — draws a line a fixed distance inside an outline. The obvious implementation moves each corner inward, and at a sharp inward-pointing notch the corner has to travel so far that it shoots across the shape instead. I replaced it with something that cannot fail that way, and I migrated the caller I had been staring at. There was a second caller two lines below it. I never looked.
What it cost was not the reprint. A border was supposed to cover that seam, and where the inset had run away, it didn't — so the part came out with black wedges in every notch. I read that as the border being too narrow and spent half a day widening it: 1.2 mm, then 1.4, then 1.6.
Rendered at all three, the wedges are identical. Not smaller. Identical.
That is a much more useful result than it looks, and I misread it three times. A fix that helps a little means keep going. A fix that changes nothing at all means the thing you are changing is not in the path that produces the symptom. There were two faults with the same symptom: one uniform, which the wider border genuinely did fix, and one ragged, which no uniform width can chase.
What ended it was drawing it. One render of the border laid over the real pattern, from models I already had, reproduced the wedges exactly and showed the width changing nothing. A few minutes against most of a day of arithmetic — on which I had already got the sign backwards twice.
Full write-up: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/inset-fix-one-caller/

item.title: Picture in Picture kept freezing, and it was the audio session
item.description:
I spent weeks on a video window that kept freezing, replaced thirteen separate pieces of the video pipeline on real hardware, and fixed none of it. The cause was audio.
The app shows a 3D printer's camera in a small floating window on an Apple TV, so you can watch a print while you watch something else. About a minute after switching which printer it was showing, that window would freeze — and so would whatever was playing behind it. Killing the app was the only thing that fixed either.
Here is the part I had missed for weeks. On Apple's platforms a floating video window is not a video feature. It is bundled together with background audio, and to get one your app has to declare itself an audio app. Mine did, and by default an app that declares itself that way takes the speakers away from everything else. It made no difference that my video is silent — the system does not care whether anyone can hear it. Rebuilding the pipeline re-claimed the speakers in the middle of someone else's playback, and everything stopped.
The fix was one option on one line. It sat there unmade because I was fairly sure it would cost me the floating window, and I could not find anywhere that said whether it does. So I built it and looked. On my device, it doesn't.
The general version: when your bug reaches into another app, stop cataloguing what might be broken in yours and start listing what the two of you share.
Full write-up, with the measurements and the one line: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/pip-freezing-audio-session/

item.title: Your teardown is queue.async { [weak self] }, so it might never run
item.description:
I spent an evening chasing a video bug, ran nine experiments against it, and refuted all nine. Then I read a piece of code none of them had touched and found a different bug: a cleanup routine that may never have been running.
An object has to release something when it shuts down, and the release has to happen on a particular background queue. So the shutdown method hands the work to that queue. And because handing work to a queue can accidentally keep objects alive forever, there's a defensive move you learn early and then type without thinking: mark the reference weak — don't keep me alive for this.
Fine, until the object is destroyed before the queue gets round to the work. The reference is already gone, the block does nothing, and the cleanup is skipped. No error, no warning, and the shutdown method returned successfully.
If what's being released is ordinary memory, none of this matters, which is exactly why the habit feels safe. Mine was a slice of the video hardware, shared with every app on the device.
The honest part: I found it by reading, not by catching it happening. There was no log line either way, because you don't instrument a path you believe is running.
So, a question rather than a rule. For every piece of cleanup you've handed off to run later: if it never runs, what doesn't get released? Memory, fine. A socket, a file handle, a lock, a piece of hardware — that needs to be guaranteed, not best-effort.
Full write-up: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/weak-self-teardown-never-runs/

item.title: Watertight, on the bed, and the wrong shape
item.description:
A part came off my 3D printer with 4 mm tongues of plastic reaching into openings that were supposed to have a clean 1.4 mm border. Every automated check I run before printing was green, and had been for months.
They were all correct. That's the part I keep thinking about.
Those checks ask whether the model is a sealed, printable solid — no holes in the surface, nothing floating in mid-air, the slicer accepts it. Not one asks whether it's the shape I actually drew. You don't usually need that second question, because you drew the thing and can see it. I generate mine in code, so nobody ever looks.
The bug was in shrinking a shape by a fixed distance. The obvious method — move every corner inward — falls apart twice: it flings sharp corners off into space, and where the outline curves tighter than the distance you're shrinking by, it turns inside out and crosses itself. A self-crossing outline still encloses something, so the model comes out sealed, printable, and wrong.
The general version isn't really about 3D printing. A validity check tells you an artefact is well-formed. It does not tell you it's the artefact you meant. If you generate your output rather than authoring it by hand, that gap is where your bugs will live.
Full write-up, with the measurements, the twenty-line test that catches it, and the check I nearly shipped instead that fires on perfectly good geometry: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/watertight-mesh-wrong-shape/

item.title: VideoToolbox emits keyframes early, and my HLS segments came out twice as long
item.description:
My video pipeline produced one segment a minute at double the length it should have been. Only on a real camera. On synthetic test video — same build, same settings, same minute — it never happened once.
The encoder was told: a keyframe at least every second. It obliged, and then it also did something I hadn't asked about. Encoders are allowed to spend keyframes early when a scene changes, and a camera pointed at a moving machine under changing light gives them scene changes constantly. A keyframe arriving 17 milliseconds too early missed my "is it time to cut?" test, so the segment stayed open until the next one — a full second later.
Two things I'd pass on.
The first is that the behaviour was documented the whole time, on the page for a *different* property, reached by a one-line "see also" from the page I was reading. I'd decided the page I was on told me what I needed. Fifteen minutes of reading both would have saved the evening.
The second is about a name. The constant I'd written for this was called "keyframe arrival tolerance" — it existed to absorb keyframes arriving slightly late. Late is one tail of a two-sided distribution, and for as long as the constant was named after that tail, the other tail wasn't something I thought to look for. Renaming it to what it actually enforces — a minimum segment length — made the bug obvious.
Name a constant after the property it enforces, not after the failure it absorbs.
Full write-up, with the before-and-after measurements and a forty-line harness that answers "which clock does this API actually use" without a device: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/videotoolbox-early-keyframes-hls-segments/

item.title: Your tvOS Top Shelf tile is cached, and reinstalling won't clear it
item.description:
I spent an evening debugging code that was already correct.
The Top Shelf tile for my tvOS app showed a placeholder instead of its image. The title was right. The progress bar was right. Just no image. I wrote two fixes, both wrong, and the thing that finally worked was rebooting the Apple TV.
The part worth knowing: the system caches the rendered tile, dedupes incoming content against that cache, and the cache survives a changed item identifier and a full uninstall and reinstall of the app.
So if you have ever shipped even one build that handed the Top Shelf a bad item, you can spend hours staring at correct code that produces a wrong screen. Nothing about the symptom suggests a cache, which is exactly why it costs so much time.
What I would carry past tvOS: all of my logging measured what the extension sent. Nothing measured what the system drew, and the two had quietly stopped being the same thing. When a fix that should work changes nothing — not the symptom, not even its shape — stop refining the fix and start asking whether your output is reaching the renderer.
Full write-up, including the exact log lines to search for and what an app extension can and can't do with an App Group: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/tvos-top-shelf-stale-cache/

item.title: Why your HealthKit widget shows zero every morning
item.description:
My iPhone widget was wrong every morning, and right the moment I opened the app.
The obvious read is that it's stale and needs to refresh harder. That was wrong, and the tell was the timestamp: it said two minutes ago. The data wasn't old. It was freshly wrong, which is a different bug with a different cause, and it rules out every fix in the refresh-scheduling family.
HealthKit encrypts its store while the phone is locked. Background wakes happen while the phone sits on a nightstand, so the reads most likely to fail are precisely the ones running unattended — and a query that fails for that reason reports no sum, identical to a day with genuinely no data.
I had written `?? 0`. So a failure became a confident zero, and every caller downstream got a number that looked like data.
The general version is the part I'd actually keep: any `??`, `try?`, or ignored error parameter whose default is 0 has made failure indistinguishable from data. Zero is uniquely dangerous because it doesn't look like an error state — it renders as a plausible, correctly formatted number that nothing downstream can flag.
Full write-up, with the fix and the second bug that refusing to publish garbage exposed: https://mcmizzle.com/blog/healthkit-widget-shows-zero/
